children: By Vaishnavi Nayel Talawadekar | Photography by Jason Henry for WSJ

By the time David and Shyama Cupp got around to renovating their makeshift, backyard guesthouse in Sacramento, Calif., it had already staged a quiet rebellion. The floors were peeling. The walls were covered in crayon. And an unmistakable, ever-present aroma of masala had settled into the 600-square-foot space, thanks to ventilation that simply wasn't up to the job.

"It was pretty much smelling like an Indian restaurant in there all day," Shyama says, laughing. That, and the absence of a dishwasher, is what finally set the renovation in motion. "My mother does like 95% of the cooking when she's here," she says. "She was hand-washing everything. We knew we at least needed to fix that."

What began as a discussion for a dishwasher grew, over the better part of a year, into a full transformation: a compact apartment dwelling unit, or ADU, with a slate roof, copper gutters and an arched Dutch door, at a cost of roughly $450,000.

David, 46, a retina surgeon, and Shyama, 43, a neuroscientist, bought the 1930s property for $1.36 million in 2019, just as Shyama relocated from Washington, D.C., to marry David. She arrived with practically nothing. "I had a couch, some IKEA chairs, and that was it," she says.

Shyama reached out to interior designers Kristine Renee and Deborah Costa of the California-based firm Jeanne Renee, whom she had followed online for months, while waiting for their calendars to open up.
"When we finally met her, she was full-term pregnant, sitting in front of one unopened Crate & Barrel box," Renee says.

The main house came first — a yearslong, room-by-room project that unfolded alongside the family's own evolution, from newlyweds to parents of a preschooler. The backyard ADU, previously home to the seller's mother, and later used as a guesthouse by the couple's own parents, was treated as an afterthought until it very much wasn't.

Shyama's parents divide their year between Tampa, Fla., and Sacramento to be with their grandson. "My mom is basically here the entire summer," Shyama says. "My dad goes back and forth to check on the house in Florida, but she stays."

During those months, the cottage — which has its own living room, bedroom and bathroom — becomes something closer to a second family kitchen than a guest suite. Shyama's family is from Gujarat, in western India, and her mother, affectionately known as Ba, cooks breakfast, lunch and dinner for the extended family most days.

The dishes are often Gujarati staples, heavy on the spices that once had nowhere to escape. These days, they have somewhere to go: a colorful quartzite counter that the designers stress-tested with a turmeric spill before installation. "We didn't want to find out the hard way," Costa says.

The kitchen has also become a de facto classroom, where the couple's 6-year-old son is learning the family's culinary inheritance. "Ba's teaching him how to make rotis," Shyama says, referring to the Indian flatbreads. "He's rolling the dough into little balls, and she's showing him how to cook it on the stove."

Tucked above a closet in the bedroom is the loft, accessed by stairs with deeply built-in drawers. Behind the closet, the designers discovered 2 feet of unused depth, which they turned into a secret, lighted hideout for the couple's son, complete with a curtain. "He and Dave found it together during construction," Costa says. "Now it's his little fort."

When the grandparents aren't in town, the cottage doesn't sit idle. On foggy winter weekends, the family holes up there for pizza, jigsaw puzzles and movies. Cupp's own parents, who live about 90 minutes away in Antioch, Calif., stay over occasionally too.
Somewhere along the way, the color and pattern in the cottage outpaced the main house, prompting what Renee calls a "small identity crisis."
"When we wrapped, Shyama looked around and asked if the main house was boring now," she says. "We had to admit — yeah, kind of."
Shyama, only half-joking, describes the moment more dramatically: "I was in tears," she says. "It's too nice over here now. We had to go back and catch the main house up."
